title: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.7 Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable
intro: Calculate and interpret center, position, spread, transformations, and potential outliers, then choose appropriate summaries.

moments.title: Mean notation
moments.text: Distinguish the sample mean from the population mean.

moments.title: Calculate a mean
moments.text: Sum the values and divide by their number.

moments.title: Find the median
moments.text: Order the observations before finding the middle.

moments.title: Quartiles
moments.text: Quartiles mark positions within the ordered data.

moments.title: Percentiles
moments.text: Percentiles describe relative position in an ordered data set.

moments.title: Range and IQR
moments.text: Range uses the extremes; IQR describes the middle half.

moments.title: Standard deviation
moments.text: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.

moments.title: Potential outliers
moments.text: Use the stated fence or standard-deviation rule.

moments.title: Calculator summaries
moments.text: Enter data, then calculate mean, median, SD, and quartiles.

moments.title: Gas mileage example
moments.text: Calculate IQR fences and compare observed values with them.

cards.name: Symmetric, no major outliers
cards.text: Mean and standard deviation describe center and spread.

cards.name: Skewed or outlying values
cards.text: Median and IQR resist extreme observations.

cards.name: Linear transformations
cards.text: Adding a constant shifts center; multiplying scales center and spread. Spread uses the absolute multiplier.

cards.name: Outlier rule
cards.text: Use the requested rule. IQR fences and a two-SD criterion need not identify the same observations.

questions.obj: Find IQR fences and assess an extreme value
questions.q: The video's 53-car sample has first quartile 17.88 mpg, third quartile 30.66 mpg, minimum 12 mpg, and maximum 55 mpg. Use IQR fences to assess the extremes.

work.text: Subtract the first quartile from the third.

steps.t: Calculate the lower and upper fences.

work.text: 12 exceeds the lower fence, while 55 exceeds the upper fence. The summary alone does not reveal every high value.

questions.answer: 55 mpg is a potential high outlier, and no observation is below the lower fence. Other high outliers require more detailed data.

questions.obj: Calculate summaries from a small data set
questions.q: Supplementary example: five package masses are 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 kg. Find the mean, median, and sample standard deviation.

steps.t: Calculate the mean and identify the middle.

work.text: The masses are already ordered. The middle value is 4 kg.

steps.t: Sum squared deviations from the mean.
Divide by one less than the sample size and take a square root.

questions.answer: The mean and median are 4 kg, and package masses typically differ from the sample mean by about 1.581 kg.

questions.q: Supplementary example: ordered times are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, and 17 minutes. Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles.

work.text: There are eight values, so average positions four and five.

steps.t: Find the median of each half.

work.text: The lower half is 2, 4, 5, 7; the upper half is 9, 11, 13, 17.

steps.t: Subtract quartiles to measure the middle-half spread.

questions.answer: The median is 8 minutes, and the middle half spans from 4.5 to 12 minutes.

sections.title: Calculate summaries from a list
sections.intro: Use the empty calculator to enter the supplementary package-mass data. These commands follow the video; the data are new.

steps.title: Enter the data
steps.suppose: we want summaries for package masses 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 kg.
do: On an empty expression line, enter `W=[2,3,4,5,6]`.
Check each entry against the data before continuing.
steps.observe: W stores all five observations. The capital letter is the same in every command.

steps.title: Find center
steps.suppose: we want the mean and median.
steps.observe: The functions summarize the list without replacing the original observations.

steps.title: Find sample spread
steps.suppose: we want the sample standard deviation.
steps.observe: Use the sample SD; it uses one fewer than the number of observations in the denominator.

steps.title: Find quartiles
steps.suppose: we want the endpoints of the middle half.
steps.observe: Quartile conventions can differ across tools for small samples. Report the calculator convention used here.

traps.title: Median position
traps.better: The median is the 15th ordered value, not necessarily the number 15.

traps.title: Standard deviation units
traps.weak: The standard deviation is 1.581 square kilograms.
traps.better: Standard deviation has the original units, kilograms; variance has squared units.

traps.title: Shifting spread
traps.weak: Adding 10 to every value increases the SD by 10.
traps.better: Adding a constant leaves SD, IQR, and range unchanged.

traps.title: Resistant does not mean fixed
traps.weak: The median never changes when data change.
traps.better: The median is resistant to extreme values, but it can change when the central ordered values change.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The two-standard-deviation rule is an alternative flagging rule, not a guarantee that a fixed percentage of all distributions lies within two SDs. The small package example supplies new data because the video's full raw data are shown on screen rather than read in the captions.

notes.label: Alternative rule.
notes.text: If the task specifies the two-SD rule, flag observations below $\bar x-2s$ or above $\bar x+2s$. This can identify different potential outliers from the IQR rule.

questions.stem: A data set is 3, 4, 5, 6, 22. Which summaries best describe typical center and spread in the presence of the high value?
why: Both are sensitive to the high value.
Both can be strongly affected by the high value.
Both are resistant to an extreme high observation.
Neither pair supplies a conventional center and spread.

questions.stem: A set of lengths has mean 12 cm and SD 3 cm. Convert every length to millimeters. What are the new mean and SD?
why: Multiplication by 10 scales both mean and SD by 10.

questions.stem: A data set has first quartile 10 and third quartile 18. What is its upper IQR fence?
why: This does not add 1.5 IQR to Q3.
IQR is 8, so the upper fence is 18+12=30.

questions.stem: A 90th percentile value is 42 minutes. Which interpretation matches the course convention?
opts: Approximately 90% are at or below 42 minutes
why: A percentile concerns cumulative position, not equality.
Percentiles locate observations within the ordered data.
The number and percentage have been reversed.
A percentile does not determine the mean.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: For a sample of workshop completion times, the mean is 30 minutes, SD is 6 minutes, and the five-number summary is 18, 24, 28, 32, 60 minutes.
parts: (a) Calculate the range, IQR, and IQR fences; assess 60 minutes.
(b) Choose resistant summaries and explain why they are appropriate.
(c) Every recorded time is multiplied by 2 and then increased by 5. Find the transformed median and SD.
sample: (a) Range=60−18=42 minutes; IQR=32−24=8 minutes. Fences are 24−12=12 and 32+12=44 minutes. 60 minutes is a potential high outlier.
(b) The median of 28 minutes and IQR of 8 minutes are resistant and are appropriate given the high outlier.
(c) The transformed median is 2(28)+5=61 minutes. The transformed SD is 2(6)=12 minutes; adding 5 does not change spread.
checklist: Explains resistance to the high outlier.

The two-standard-deviation rule is an alternative flagging rule, not a guarantee that a fixed percentage of all distributions lies within two SDs. The small package example supplies new data because the video's full raw data are shown on screen rather than read in the captions.

Linear transformations are a CED supplement. The video link attached to the transformation checks reviews standard deviation rather than demonstrating a transformation. Calculator commands use a new five-value list rather than reconstructing the video table.
